t1-value-chain.title: From output to value
t1-value-chain.caption: The project delivers the output. Outcomes, benefits and value happen in the business, mostly after handover, which is why benefits need an owner who stays.
t1-value-chain.alt: Four boxes left to right joined by arrows: Output, Outcome, Benefit, Value. Under each, the booking example: system delivered; patients book online; fewer missed appointments; worth more than it cost. A bracket under Output reads Delivered by the project; a bracket under the other three reads Realised in the business, after handover.

shapes.t: Realised in the business, mostly after handover

t2-timeline.title: Milestones in the discipline
t2-timeline.caption: Planning-and-control methods came first; adaptive methods and principle-based standards came later, as the field put uncertainty and people at the centre.
t2-timeline.alt: A timeline from 1900 to 2025 with six marked points: 1910s Gantt chart; 1957 to 1958 critical path method and PERT; 1969 PMI founded; 1996 first PMBOK Guide and PRINCE2; 2001 Agile Manifesto; 2021 principle-based standard.

t3-competencies.title: Three kinds of competence
t3-competencies.caption: PMI's talent triangle. Good practice draws on all three at once: a risk conversation with a sponsor needs technique, business sense and the skill to get a decision made.
t3-competencies.alt: A triangle of three boxes joined by lines: Ways of working at the top (planning, scheduling, methods), Power skills at bottom left (leading, communicating, negotiating), Business acumen at bottom right (strategy, finance, customers). In the middle: Project professional.

shapes.t:
Ways of working
planning, scheduling, methods

t4-hierarchy.title: From strategy to delivery
t4-hierarchy.caption: The portfolio chooses the work, programmes coordinate related projects for combined benefits, and projects hand their outputs to operations.
t4-hierarchy.alt: Strategy at the top feeds a portfolio. The portfolio contains a programme made of two projects, a stand-alone project, and operations. Dashed arrows show projects handing outputs over to operations.

shapes.t: Portfolio: choose and balance the work

t4-structures.title: Who holds the authority
t4-structures.caption: From functional to projectised organisations, the project manager's authority over people and budget grows, and so does the team's focus on the project.
t4-structures.alt: Five bars of increasing height labelled Functional, Weak matrix, Balanced matrix, Strong matrix and Projectised, showing the project manager's authority rising from low to high.

t5-principles.title: Twelve principles
t5-principles.caption: The principles apply whatever the approach. They are not steps: each is a lens for judging a decision, and good decisions usually satisfy several at once.
t5-principles.alt: Twelve boxes in three rows of four: Stewardship, Team, Stakeholders, Value; Systems thinking, Leadership, Tailoring, Quality; Complexity, Risk, Adaptability and resilience, Change.

t6-spectrum.title: Four ways to develop a product
t6-spectrum.caption: Two questions place an approach: how often the product reaches its users, and how much it is expected to change as people learn.
t6-spectrum.alt: A two-by-two grid. Across: frequency of delivery, from once to often. Up: degree of change, from low to high. Bottom left Predictive: plan once, deliver once. Bottom right Incremental: plan once, deliver in pieces. Top left Iterative: refine through cycles, deliver once. Top right Agile: refine and deliver in short cycles.

shapes.t:
Iterative
refine through cycles,
deliver once

Agile
refine and deliver
in short cycles

Incremental
plan once,
deliver in pieces

t7-scrum.title: One Scrum sprint
t7-scrum.caption: Planning sets a sprint goal, the team works with a daily scrum, the review shows the increment and feeds the backlog, and the retrospective improves how the next sprint runs.
t7-scrum.alt: Product backlog, then Sprint planning, then the Sprint of one to four weeks with a daily scrum, then Sprint review, then the Increment. A dashed line from the review returns to the product backlog: feedback reorders it. Below, the Sprint retrospective feeds back into the next sprint planning.

t7-kanban.title: A Kanban board
t7-kanban.caption: Each column is a stage; the limits cap how much work can sit in each one, so the team finishes work before starting more.
t7-kanban.alt: A board of four columns: To do with four cards, In progress with a limit of three and three cards, Review with a limit of two and two cards, and Done with three cards. Work moves right only when the next column has room.

shapes.t: Work moves right only when the next column has room

t8-uncertainty.title: Two kinds of uncertainty
t8-uncertainty.caption: The less agreed the requirements and the less known the technology, the more the work calls for short feedback loops. Adapted from Ralph Stacey's agreement and certainty matrix.
t8-uncertainty.alt: A chart with technology from known to unknown along the bottom and requirements from agreed to unclear up the side. Nested regions from the bottom left corner: Simple, suited to predictive; Complicated, predictive or hybrid; Complex, adaptive; and Chaotic at the far corner, act first then stabilise.

t9-start.title: How a project earns the right to start
t9-start.caption: The need comes before the solution; the business case argues for one option; a decision authorises it; the charter records the agreement that planning builds on.
t9-start.alt: Five boxes left to right: Need (problem, opportunity or obligation), Business case (options, costs, benefits, risks), Decision (approve, defer or reject), Charter (authorises the project, names the project manager), Planning (detail built on the charter).

shapes.t:
authorises the project,
names the project
manager

t10-wbs.title: Part of a work breakdown structure
t10-wbs.caption: Deliverables at the second level, work packages at the lowest. Project management is part of the work, so it has a branch of its own.
t10-wbs.alt: A tree. At the top, Online booking project. Below it four deliverables: Booking system (patient screens, reminders, testing), Records interface (interface build, vendor testing), Rollout and training (pilot clinic, clinic waves, staff training), and Project management (planning, reporting).

t11-network.title: The critical path
t11-network.caption: Two paths lead from A to D. The longer one, A–C–D, sets the finish at day 11; B can slip two days without moving the end date.
t11-network.alt: A network of four activities. A takes 3 days and leads to B (4 days) and C (6 days), which both lead to D (2 days). A–C–D is highlighted as the critical path of 11 days; A–B–D takes 9 days, so B has 2 days of float.

t12-budget.title: Building the budget
t12-budget.caption: Estimates plus contingency make the cost baseline that performance is measured against; adding management reserve gives the total budget.
t12-budget.alt: Three stacked layers: work package estimates at the bottom, contingency reserves for known risks above them, and management reserve for unknown risks on top. A bracket marks the bottom two as the cost baseline, controlled by the project manager; a larger bracket marks all three as the project budget, where management approves use of the reserve.

shapes.t:
Cost baseline:

project manager

Project budget:
management

t12-evm.title: Earned value at month four
t12-evm.caption: Work worth 200 should be done; work worth 160 is done; it cost 180. The project is behind (EV below PV) and over cost (AC above EV); at this efficiency it would finish near 450 against a budget of 400.
t12-evm.alt: A chart of cumulative cost against months. The planned value curve rises in an S shape to 400 at month 8. At the status date, month 4, planned value is 200, earned value 160 and actual cost 180. A dashed forecast continues the actual cost to about 450 at month 10.

t13-coq.title: The cost of quality
t13-coq.caption: Money spent on prevention and appraisal is the cost of conformance; failures found inside or outside the organisation are the cost of non-conformance, and usually the larger.
t13-coq.alt: Two groups. Cost of conformance: prevention (training, reviews, standards) and appraisal (testing, inspection). Cost of non-conformance: internal failure (rework, retest, delay) and external failure (support, recalls, reputation). An arrow beneath runs left to right: the further right a defect is dealt with, the more it costs.

shapes.t: The further right a defect is dealt with, the more it costs

t13-control.title: A control chart
t13-control.caption: Points between the control limits show the process's normal variation. A point outside them, or a run of seven on one side of the mean, signals a special cause worth investigating.
t13-control.alt: Twenty measurements plotted over time between an upper control limit, a mean line and a lower control limit. Seven consecutive points sit above the mean, and one point lies above the upper control limit; both are highlighted.

shapes.t: seven in a row above the mean

t14-matrix.title: A probability and impact matrix
t14-matrix.caption: Risks are placed by how likely they are and how much they would matter. The top right corner gets attention and responses first.
t14-matrix.alt: A three-by-three grid with probability up the side (low, medium, high) and impact along the bottom (low, medium, high). Cells shade from green at low-low to red at high-high. Examples: vendor interface late is high probability and high impact; key developer leaves is medium probability and high impact; room booking clash is low probability and low impact.

t15-risk.title: Who carries the cost risk
t15-risk.caption: Fixed-price contracts leave overruns mainly with the seller; cost-reimbursable ones mainly with the buyer. Time and materials sits between.
t15-risk.alt: Contract types in a row from seller risk to buyer risk: firm fixed price, fixed price with economic price adjustment, fixed price incentive fee, time and materials, cost plus incentive fee, cost plus award fee, cost plus fixed fee. The first three are grouped as fixed price, the last three as cost-reimbursable.

t16-change.title: Integrated change control
t16-change.caption: Every change is recorded and assessed across scope, time, cost, quality and risk before someone with the authority decides; approved changes update all the plans and are communicated.
t16-change.alt: A flow: Change request, Log it, Assess impact on everything, Decide (authority or board). If approved: Update plans and baselines, Communicate, Implement and verify. A dashed line from the decision leads to Rejected or deferred: record, explain.

t17-burnup.title: A burnup chart
t17-burnup.caption: Done and total scope are drawn separately, so new scope shows as a step in its own line instead of looking like the team slowed down.
t17-burnup.alt: Two lines over twelve iterations. Total scope is flat at 100 and steps up to 120 at iteration 4. Work done rises steadily to 66 by iteration 6, and a dashed forecast meets the scope line around iteration 11.
